books.section: Topic 6.6 The Rise of Industrial Capitalism
Industrialization, Corporate Consolidation, and the Gospel of Wealth

options.misconception: A building this large filled orders from across the country, not only from Chicago.
options.text: That it sold goods only in Chicago

options.misconception: A warehouse this size stored factory goods for shipment, not handmade goods.
options.text: That it made all its goods by hand

options.misconception: A company does not build a towered headquarters while losing money; the building shows success.

options.text: That it handled a huge volume of goods

rationales.A: The building stood in Chicago, but its catalogs reached customers far away, so its market was national.
rationales.B: Background: the goods Ward sold were factory-made. The building stored them; it did not make them by hand.
rationales.C: A firm builds a landmark headquarters when business is growing, not when it is failing.
rationales.D: A multi-story building with a tall tower, called one of the sights of the city, fits a firm that stored and shipped goods in great numbers.
rationales.general:
Read the building as evidence.
1. The building fills the picture: many floors, a tall tower, and a caption calling it a sight of the city.
2. A mail-order house needs room to store goods and fill orders.
3. Only a firm handling a huge volume needs a building this large.
4. So the size itself shows a national business, not a small shop.
Remember: the size of a firm’s building can show the size of its business.

stem: What does the size of the Montgomery Ward building suggest about the company?

stimulus.text: A stereoscopic view of the Montgomery Ward and Company establishment in Chicago, a huge multi-story building with a tall tower rising over the neighboring blocks. The caption calls it “one of the sights of the city,” and the building’s many windows show floor after floor of goods.
